references.text: Isaiah prophesies about the destruction of Zion: 'Her gates shall sigh and mourn, and she shall sit on the ground, plundered' (Isa 3:26). This reflects Jesus' words about Jerusalem's coming destruction.

Hosea speaks of Samaria's guilt and judgment: 'Samaria must bear her guilt, for she has been rebellious against her God. They shall fall by the sword; their little ones shall be dashed in pieces' (Hos 14:1). The motif of children being affected in the city's destruction echoes in Jesus' prophecy.
The psalm about Babylon speaks of dashing little children against the rock (Ps 137:9). The verb ἐδαφιοῦσιν (dash to the ground) in Luke 19:44 carries the same brutal image of destruction.

Micah prophesies that 'Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem become a heap of ruins' (Mic 3:12). This prophecy about Jerusalem's total destruction corresponds with Jesus' words that not one stone will be left upon another.

Daniel prophesies that the city and sanctuary will be destroyed (Dan 9:24-26). The prophecy concerning Jerusalem's destruction after the coming of the Anointed One has direct relevance to Jesus' words that Jerusalem did not know its time of visitation.

Jesus repeats the prophecy about the temple's destruction: 'There will come days when not one stone will be left upon another without being thrown down' (Luke 21:6). The expression 'stone upon stone' (λίθον ἐπὶ λίθον) is identical to Luke 19:44.
In Matt 24:1-2, Jesus prophesies about the temple's destruction using the same expression: 'Not one stone will be left here upon another without being thrown down.'

Zechariah praises God who 'has visited and redeemed his people' (Luke 1:68). The word ἐπισκοπή (visitation) in 19:44 stands in contrast to this: Jerusalem did not know its time of visitation when God came to redeem.
Jesus says, 'If you had only known on this day what would bring you peace!' (Luke 19:42). This verse provides the direct context for verse 44 – Jerusalem did not know its time of visitation.
Peter exhorts right conduct 'on the day of visitation' (1 Pet 2:12). The word ἐπισκοπή is used concerning God's visitation, in the same way as in Jesus' lament over Jerusalem.

Jeremiah says about Jerusalem, 'They should be ashamed, for they have done detestable things... Therefore they shall fall' (Jer 6:15). The prophecy concerns that the people did not know the Lord's time of visitation and the consequences thereof.
